P1.evidence: P1a partial — the application is acknowledged but nothing from it is reflected back: 'So, look, I saw your application. Now, I want to get a little bit in detail on what you're trying to achieve.' P1b partial — two of the four frame elements delivered ('what you're trying to achieve and how can we possibly help you achieving that'), missing where you are now and what you need. P1c miss — no frame agreement, no 'does that work?'. P1d hit — the open question is asked, though narrowed to training: 'walk me through, like, in terms of fitness, what do you do currently?'

P2.evidence: P2e hit — the opening question produced an unusually complete training picture: pull-ups, EMOMs, burpees, kettlebells, dumbbells, running intervals, rucking, mountain biking, indoor cycling and canoe racing. P2f hit — 'How do you feel like how far off you are from your goal?' produced an honest self-assessment of mediocre returns on high effort, which became the spine of the whole call. P2g hit — nutrition asked properly and followed up: 'Could you walk me through how does it look like for you right now?' then 'could you look at what your typical day of eating looks like?'. P2d partial and important — the rep did probe when the prospect said running hurt ('Why is it painful?'), which surfaced bilateral torn ACLs, but he never asked the injuries-and-limitations question directly and never followed up on the ACLs at all: whether they were surgically reconstructed, what they rule out, or how they interact with ballistic loading. P2a miss — age (turning 40) and weight (190 lb, up from 180) were both volunteered inside other answers; height never established. P2b miss — that he is starting a company only emerged forty minutes later while resisting the price, and it turned out to be the actual cashflow constraint; asking at P2 would have surfaced it before the offer. P2c miss — health conditions never asked. P2h miss — sleep never mentioned by either party, despite the rep later citing sleep as a foundation during the nutrition pillar. P2i miss — energy never asked.

P3.evidence: The deep why was reached, but this prospect arrived with it already articulated and did most of the work himself. P3a/P3b partial — one broad question stands in for the scripted sequence: 'in your own words, what would be the biggest goal that you want to reach?', which produced the grandfather-at-seventy frame, the 15-20 lb target and the accountability insight all at once. P3f partial — the rep did not ask 'who else does that impact?' but did open the door with 'How old are your kids?' and then worked it. P3g hit and well done — he built the timeline himself ('So there's a lot of years that you need to be in shape', 'a lot of rolling on the ground in front of you', 'your back needs to be in check') and tied it to the Michigan outdoor life, drawing out the 60 acres, the daily family hikes and teaching the kids to ski. P3h hit — the reflect-and-confirm move ran cleanly, applied to the root cause rather than the goal: 'the structure, and being coached, and having a program that you can stick to, this is the main thing... Would that be fair?' answered 'I think so, yeah.' P3c miss — no 'something physical you want to do but can't', which was odd given a canoe race is his stated next target. P3d miss — the outside-the-physical bridge never asked. P3e miss — 'when you're moving better, what does that actually do for you?' never asked.

P4.evidence: Strong. P4a hit — past attempts surfaced and then probed: five years training alone, prior coaching in both fitness and business, and the rep followed the competitive thread with 'the other coaches that you were looking into, they're also like doing kettlebells or different stuff?'. P4b hit — the outcome is stated plainly: 'over the last five years, I've been working out on my own, and I'm getting mediocre results because I'm not quite able to push myself hard enough.' P4c hit — the reason it does not stick was drawn out rather than assumed. P4d hit — the single blocker was isolated and confirmed via the P3h reflect-back. P4e hit — the prospect named the gap in his own words repeatedly and precisely: 'it's easy for me to self-negotiate with myself', 'I'm not pushing myself that extra 20%', 'it's easy to cut the sets a little short. Nobody's telling me what to do. Nobody's going to know.' P4f miss — the scripted 'the information isn't the problem, why can't you stick to it on your own?' frame was never delivered. It was arguably unnecessary here since the prospect had already conceded the point unprompted, but the script credits asking.

P5.evidence: Phase 5 was never run in position. The prospect supplied his own consequence unprompted at 00:05:00 — 'I'm 190 now... I don't want to continue to do this and be 200, 210, 220, and then way out of shape. It's a slippery slope' — which the script explicitly does not credit to the rep. P5a partial rather than miss only because the rep did eventually deliver a consequence frame, but sixteen minutes after the price and as an objection handler rather than as a phase: 'In 5, 10 years, 15 years, are you going to still remember this 6K that you spent? When you're going to be freaking healthy and showing up for your family every single day? Really? Or on your deathbed?' That was the most effective moment of the call — the prospect responded 'That's a good point... I like that pitch' — which is precisely the argument for running it BEFORE the number, where it would have been weighing against the price rather than chasing it. P5b, P5c and P5d all miss: no 'are you willing to settle for that?', no 'why not?', no line in the sand.

P6.evidence: P6b hit — asked and answered before price: 'if we can figure out all the technical logistical details, are you fully committed to showing up and doing the work?' / 'Oh, yeah, for sure.' P6a hit and, unusually, followed up properly — 'do you feel like what we've gone through today can actually get you to your goals, like you're going to lose extra pounds and have something that you learned for life?' The prospect hedged with 'Yeah, I think it probably would', and the rep caught the hedge and pressed it: 'Probably?' then 'What, like in your mind, like what could happen that it wouldn't work?' That produced the real answer — that the doubt was self-directed, not programme-directed. This is the best-executed belief check in the batch. P6c partial — the yes at P6b was explicitly conditional ('if we can make a deal, then yeah, I'd be there for sure') and the rep treated it as unqualified, moving straight to the investment. That conditional was the signal that price was unresolved, and the script's instruction is to return to Phase 5 when hesitation surfaces rather than proceed. Sequencing note: as on every call in this batch, the pillars were presented before the commitment check.

P11.evidence: Payment and onboarding were unreachable — the prospect declined to decide, repeatedly and explicitly. Scored N/A so the rep is not penalised. The handover, however, was the best in the batch and should be the template: the rep established the channel ('You use WhatsApp?'), sent a test message live and had it confirmed ('Got it'), pinned the time zone ('You're in Eastern?') and agreed a specific callback slot ('Can I reach out to you like around 4 p.m.?'). Compare with the smanian call the same day, where a warm prospect with a discounted offer was left with no booked next step at all.

objection_plays.detail: Trigger raised at least six times across fifteen minutes and worked hard. Three scripted moves ran: the belief question ('do you feel like what we've gone through today can actually get you to your goals?'), the follow-up probe on what makes him feel it can/can't ('what could happen that it wouldn't work?'), and the what's-actually-coming-up isolation ('what's stopping you? Is it that the budget is tight or what is it?'). Four did not: 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is'; 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here — when do you make a different decision?'; 'that man you want to be, how does HE decide right now?'; and the final 'are you sure? Nothing else keeping you from being 100% in?'. The third of those is the notable omission — the rep had spent ten minutes building a grandfather-at-seventy identity frame and never converted it into a decision frame. In its place he used two pressure variants that are not in the playbook — 'You want me to give up on you that easily?' and 'You cannot or you don't want to commit?' — which the prospect, a salesperson himself, named as tactics rather than answered.

Two of six moves, one of them the most important. The rep opened badly by dismissing the objection before hearing it — 'So don't give me the, the, the wife objections' — and the prospect pushed back ('I understand there's a wife objection, but there really is'). He then recovered well and ran the permission-versus-finances move cleanly: 'is it really that you're asking her for permission, or you're just figuring out the financials?', which produced the useful concession 'mostly figuring out the financials, but... it's a little bit of both'. He also ran 'when you talk to her, what do you think, what she's going to say about it?'. Missing: 'money aside, do you personally feel this CAN get you to your goal?' (run later, out of position, as part of OA); 'is there any reason she would NOT want you stronger and less in pain?'; 'this isn't a joint decision like buying a house — is that responsibility hers or yours?'; and critically the deposit-with-full-refund fallback. That last omission matters most here, because the prospect twice signalled he was looking for a structure to get to yes — 'let me see if I can put together something that I can get to' — and a deposit was the obvious answer sitting unused in the script.

The isolation ran and ran well — 'Is it the money thing or something else that you're still not sure about the value that you're getting?' — and produced the cleanest possible answer: the value was not in question, only the size of the outgoing. The break-it-up offer ran twice ('we can talk about how to structure that', 'So what's your take? You want to split it?') but was never converted into an actual structure, and the rep did not return to it after the prospect failed to bite. Not one of the six financial-picture questions ran: no cash on hand, no monthly surplus, no credit cards, no available credit, no investments. The rep instead asserted 'So the money is there. That's for sure' on the strength of two volunteered $10,000 purchases, and the prospect did not dispute it. The $500/month competitor anchor, raised twice, was never addressed by the OC play or by anything else.

Two of six moves, and the two that matter, both delivered well. The certainty frame ran near-verbatim: 'Would it be fair to say that you're looking for certainty that if you do what Trevor teaches would actually get you there?' The prospect engaged seriously with it, reasoning through a fast/cheap/guaranteed trade-off and concluding certainty was his highest priority. The rep then closed with the how-will-you-know move: 'how can actually you be certain if you don't try, especially with fitness, right? Because it's your body.' The prospect conceded — 'Agreed. Yeah, I mean, that's some logic there is like, if I continue to not get what I want, and then I would regret the certainty of not being able to do it.' Missing: pleasure-versus-pain, the bridge, the plane analogy and the burned-before frame. The rep also introduced a guarantee here, which is not an OE move and which is separately flagged.

A genuine timing objection was present and went entirely unworked: 'I'm starting a company and I'm just starting to take a salary and that's a huge part of it.' None of the OD moves ran. The rep reframed it into a desire question instead ('is it the right thing to do in terms of finances or actually doing it?'), which skipped past the constraint rather than dissolving it. 'Things never slow down — when does it actually become the right time?' was directly available and unused.

SCRIPT GAP — the self-spend threshold, now the third instance in this batch. Stated with unusual clarity: 'I don't think I have any questions about the value... I just have to get used to the fact of having $6,000 go out of my bank accounts pretty much.' The OC play is built for a buyer who cannot pay; this is a buyer who can pay and cannot yet press the button. The rep improvised the right shape of answer — the future-regret frame — and it visibly moved the prospect. That improvisation should be written into the playbook as a formal play, because reps are currently reaching for discounts (smanian) or financing (Arturo) when the correct tool is a regret frame.

SCRIPT GAP — a cheaper coaching alternative that was adequate. The $500/month prior coach is a direct price anchor at 50% of the effective monthly rate, raised twice and never answered. This is the same gap already logged from the Badrane Hriouch call and repeated on the smanian call in this batch. There is no scripted way to justify the premium over a functioning cheaper coach, and here the rep did not attempt one.

SCRIPT GAP — selling to a professional salesperson who narrates the plays in real time. 'I know all your strategies, bro. I sell people every day', 'I appreciate the sales pitch it's good, I like selling', 'I close every day.' Every pressure move was identified out loud and defused socially rather than answered. The playbook has no guidance for a buyer who is inside the frame, and the rep's most effective moments here were the two that were not recognisable as technique: the future-regret question and his own hip dysplasia story.

SCRIPT GAP — an actively competitive process. The prospect disclosed he was evaluating at least two other coaches, one of whom he had previously used and one who had not yet replied: 'I like to at least talk to a few different people.' No competitive-differentiation play exists and none was run. The rep asked one useful qualifying question ('they're also like doing kettlebells or different stuff?') and then never used the answer, which was that neither competitor does kettlebells and that the prospect prefers Trevor's content.

notes: The best-fought call in the batch and it still did not close, which makes it the most diagnostic. Discovery, root cause and the belief check were all genuinely strong — catching the 'probably' hedge and asking what could go wrong is the single best piece of technique in this batch. Three things cost the deal, and none of them are effort. First, Phase 5 was never run in position: the deathbed frame that finally moved him was deployed sixteen minutes AFTER the price, when it should have been the thing the price was weighed against. Second, the $500/month anchor was stated twice and never once addressed, so the prospect spent the whole objection sequence comparing $6,000 against $3,000 of prior coaching with no counter-argument supplied. Third, having offered to split the payment twice, the rep never actually built a structure — for a founder just starting to draw a salary, a deposit or an instalment schedule was the entire answer and it was left on the table. Separately and urgently: a guarantee was improvised mid-objection and its scope widened within thirty seconds from a strength metric to a weight-loss outcome. That needs a ruling before it is said again.
